questions.question: The surah opens with an oath by 'al-Tur.' Which sacred location does this refer to, and why is it invoked here?
options: A. Mount Uhud, site of the famous early Muslim battle, invoked to honor the martyrs who fell there
B. Mount Sinai, the place where Allah spoke directly to Prophet Moses, evoking divine communication
C. Mount Hira, where the first Quranic revelation descended upon the Prophet Muhammad
D. Mount Arafat, the central site of the Hajj, invoked to honor the pilgrimage rite
questions.explanation: Al-Tur refers to Mount Sinai (Jabal Musa), where Allah spoke directly to Prophet Moses and delivered the Torah. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah swears by al-Tur because it is intimately associated with divine revelation and the honor of prophethood, connecting the Quran's message to that earlier sacred history of divine communication.

questions.question: True or false: The classical scholars Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, and Qatada all agreed that the 'kitabin mastur' (inscribed Book) in verse 2 refers to the Preserved Tablet upon which all of Allah's decrees are recorded.
questions.explanation: Al-Tabari in Jami al-Bayan records that the most prominent view, attributed to Ibn Abbas and affirmed by the majority of early exegetes, is that 'kitabin mastur' refers to the Preserved Tablet. Ibn Kathir leans toward the same view, noting it gives the greatest rhetorical force to the oath sequence: Allah is swearing by a cosmic, pre-eternal divine record.

questions.question: Verse 4 describes Al-Bayt al-Mamur, the 'Frequented House.' What is this, and where is it located according to the Prophet's own account?
options: A. The original Kaaba built by Adam, buried beneath the present Kaaba in Mecca
B. The celestial counterpart of the Kaaba located in the seventh heaven, visited daily by seventy thousand angels who never return
C. A sacred mosque in Jerusalem visited perpetually by the souls of the prophets
D. A spiritual symbol for the heart of the believer, which must be kept pure through constant worship
questions.explanation: According to the hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari and Sahih Muslim, the Prophet saw Al-Bayt al-Mamur during the night journey and was told that seventy thousand angels visit it every single day to worship and circumambulate, and once an angel has visited it, that angel will never return. Ibn Kathir confirms it is in the seventh heaven directly above the earthly Kaaba.

questions.question: Which additional detail about Al-Bayt al-Mamur does Ibn Kathir record through multiple chains of transmission from the Prophet's night journey?
options: A. It was built by the angels in the first heaven before Adam was created
B. The Prophet Ibrahim was seen leaning against Al-Bayt al-Mamur during the night journey
C. The entire angelic host circumambulates it once every Friday night
D. It will descend to earth and merge with the earthly Kaaba before the Day of Resurrection
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir records through multiple chains of transmission that the Prophet saw Prophet Ibrahim leaning against Al-Bayt al-Mamur during the night journey. Ibn Kathir interprets this as a sign of Ibrahim's special status as the original builder of the earthly Kaaba and his intimate connection with its heavenly counterpart.

questions.question: True or false: Verse 7 ('the punishment of your Lord will certainly occur') is the grammatical answer to the chain of six oaths that precedes it in verses 1 through 6.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explains that verses 1 through 6 form the oath (al-qasam) and verse 7 is the answer to that oath (jawab al-qasam). This is a well-known rhetorical device in classical Arabic. The Arabic particle 'inna,' combined with the emphatic 'la-waqi'un' (will certainly fall), creates a triple layer of certainty that gives maximum weight to the sworn statement.

questions.question: Muhammad al-Sha'rawi observed that verse 7 serves a specific psychological purpose. What did he identify as its primary effect on the listener?
options: A. To provide a detailed chronology of when the Day of Judgment will arrive
B. To awaken the dormant conscience, severing the path of doubt so the hearer cannot delay repentance by doubting the reckoning
C. To demonstrate the Quran's linguistic superiority over Arabic poetry of the Quraysh
D. To establish a legal precedent for oath-taking in Islamic jurisprudence
questions.explanation: Muhammad al-Sha'rawi emphasized that the certainty in this verse is meant to awaken the dormant conscience. The human being often delays repentance because he doubts the reckoning, but this verse severs that path of doubt entirely. Ibn Uthaymeen similarly argued that genuine belief in 'la-waqi'un' should transform how a Muslim lives each day, producing not theoretical belief but an active awareness of accountability.

questions.question: What does the term 'al-mukadhdhibun' in verse 11 specifically indicate about those who receive the 'wayl' (woe)?
options: A. People who were geographically isolated and never received the Prophet's message
B. People who followed their ancestors without reflection but without malicious intent
C. Those who actively and deliberately rejected divine truth after it had been made clear to them
D. People who outwardly professed faith while inwardly concealing disbelief
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari in Jami al-Bayan analyzes 'wayl' as comprehensive destruction directed at those who deliberately rejected the truth brought by the Prophet Muhammad. Ibn Kathir emphasizes that 'al-mukadhdhibun' refers specifically to those who rejected the Quran, the Day of Resurrection, and the prophethood of Muhammad, implying deliberate choice against clear evidence rather than mere ignorance.

questions.question: True or false: Al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb noted that the passive voice 'yudauna' (they will be thrust) in verse 13 deliberately removes all agency from the deniers, emphasizing their complete powerlessness after a lifetime of arrogant self-assertion.
questions.explanation: Fakhr al-Din al-Razi in Mafatih al-Ghayb specifically observes that the passive voice 'yudauna' removes any agency from the deniers, emphasizing their utter powerlessness on that Day after a lifetime of arrogant self-assertion against Allah. Ibn Kathir similarly records that multiple classical scholars including Mujahid and Ash-Shabi interpreted this word as meaning violent, repeated, forceful thrusting without mercy.

questions.question: Verse 17 identifies the inhabitants of Paradise as 'al-muttaqeen.' What does this specifically indicate about the path that earned them that reward?
options: A. They were born into righteous families with a hereditary predisposition to faith
B. They cultivated genuine God-consciousness throughout their lives, carefully guarding against sin and fulfilling their obligations
C. They performed the most publicly visible charitable acts in their communities
D. They were scholars who memorized the entire Quran and devoted themselves exclusively to religious study
questions.explanation: Imam al-Qurtubi notes that Allah specifically named the believers as 'muttaqeen' to indicate that their entry into paradise is a direct result of their taqwa, which was their shield in this world and becomes their key to paradise. Imam al-Tabari explains that taqwa in its fullest sense encompasses belief in the unseen, performing salat, spending in Allah's path, and avoiding what He has prohibited throughout daily life.

questions.question: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects on the social dimension of Paradise depicted in verse 21 and surrounding verses. What key insight does he draw about the nature of life in Paradise?
options: A. Paradise is a solitary spiritual experience where each soul communes with Allah in isolation
B. Paradise is deeply communal and relational, with believers reclining on thrones facing each other and families reunited in shared joy
C. Paradise is organized around continuous collective worship with no time for personal interaction
D. The social dimension of Paradise is identical to the social structures of the best Muslim societies on earth
questions.explanation: Sayyid Qutb in Fi Zilal al-Quran reflects that Paradise is not a solitary spiritual experience but a deeply communal and relational one. He notes that the Quran consistently portrays paradise as a place of joyful human connection, with believers facing each other on arranged thrones and families reunited in faith. Wahbah al-Zuhayli similarly emphasizes that verse 21 shows family bonds rooted in shared faith extending into eternity.

questions.question: True or false: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen taught that fear of Allah expressed within the family context is the highest form of taqwa, because it is exercised without a public audience, purely between the servant and his Lord.
questions.explanation: Sheikh Ibn Uthaymeen commented that fear of Allah within the family context is the highest form of that fear, because it is exercised without an audience, without social praise, purely between the servant and his Lord. This is drawn from verse 26, where the people of Paradise recall having been 'fearful among our families' in the worldly life, demonstrating that their taqwa permeated private domestic life, not just public worship.

questions.question: In verse 29, Allah refutes two specific accusations the Quraysh were using to dismiss the Prophet. What were those two accusations?
options: A. That he was a sorcerer (sahir) and an imposter claiming foreign learning
B. That he was a soothsayer (kahin) receiving information from jinn, and a madman (majnun)
C. That he was an arrogant tribal leader and a poet who composed for wealth
D. That he was a liar (kadhdhab) and a political agitator against the Quraysh chiefs
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir explains that the Meccan disbelievers accused the Prophet of being a 'kahin,' a soothsayer who received information from jinn, and a 'majnun,' one possessed by madness. Allah categorically refutes both, with the phrase 'by the favor of your Lord' signaling that the Prophet's freedom from these defects is itself a divine gift. Imam Razi notes the irony: the Quran's very excellence caused them to reach for these labels.

questions.question: The challenge in verse 34 to produce 'a discourse like it' belongs to what broader Quranic phenomenon, and what has been its historical outcome according to Ibn Kathir?
options: A. The 'i'rab,' a grammatical challenge; it was met by the grammarians of Basra within a century
B. The 'tahaddi,' the challenge of inimitability; it was issued over fourteen centuries ago and has never been successfully met
C. The 'tawatur,' a proof of transmission; it was accepted by the Quraysh after witnessing the Battle of Badr
D. The 'ijaz al-ilmi,' a scientific challenge; it was addressed by Muslim scientists in the medieval period
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir connects this verse to the broader Quranic challenge known as the 'tahaddi,' where disbelievers are repeatedly invited to produce even one chapter comparable to the Quran. Ibn Kathir also notes that the Prophet was known throughout Mecca as 'al-Amin' (the trustworthy) before his prophethood, making the fabrication charge historically incoherent. The tahaddi, issued over fourteen centuries ago, has never been successfully met.

questions.question: True or false: Ibn Kathir records that when Jubayr ibn Mutim heard the Prophet reciting verse 35 in the Maghrib prayer, it so struck his heart that he subsequently accepted Islam.
questions.explanation: Ibn Kathir relates the account of Jubayr ibn Mutim, who came to Medina before accepting Islam and heard the Prophet reciting Surah al-Tur. When the Prophet reached verse 35, Jubayr later said it felt as though his heart would fly out of his chest. He subsequently accepted Islam, illustrating the verse's immediate rational and spiritual impact as a proof for the existence of Allah through the logic of contingent existence.

questions.question: Verse 49, the final verse of the surah, commands the Prophet to glorify Allah during 'a portion of the night' and at 'idbar al-nujum.' How did the majority of classical scholars identify 'idbar al-nujum'?
options: A. The middle of the night when the stars are at their peak brightness
B. After Isha prayer, the first hour of the night
C. The pre-dawn period just before Fajr, when the stars begin to fade at the approach of dawn
D. After sunset when the first stars appear on the horizon
questions.explanation: Imam al-Tabari records a consensus among the Companions and Tabi'in, including Ibn Abbas and Ibn Masud, that 'idbar al-nujum' refers to the two voluntary sunnah rak'ahs before Fajr, performed while the stars are setting at the approach of dawn. Ibn Kathir supports this with the hadith from Sahih Muslim in which the Prophet said: 'The two rak'ahs before Fajr are better than this world and all it contains.'
